messages.subject: inlabru: replicating effects
messages.subject_clean: inlabru: replicating effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am trying to use inlabru for multiple likelihoods. In particular, I am trying to understand how to conduct some features that R-INLA provides for copying and replicating effects. Here a reproducible example for the copy one (using the scale parameter feature) assuming different intercepts:

# Simulate data: 2 groups with same AR1 param

n = 500

rho <- 0.8

intercept <- c(1, -1)

x1 = arima.sim(n=n, model=list(ar=c(rho)))

x2 = arima.sim(n=n, model=list(ar=c(rho)))

sd <- c(0.01, 0.01)

# Gaussian observations

set.seed(10)

y1 = rnorm(n, mean = intercept[1] + x1, sd = sd[1])

y2 = rnorm(n, mean = intercept[2] + x2, sd = sd[2])

mydata <- data.frame(y1, y2, t = 1:n)

#Effects

cmp1 <- ~ Intercept1 +     Intercept2 +

    + arima1(t, model = "ar1") +

    + arima2(t, copy = "arima1", fixed = FALSE)

 #Formula for each linear predictor

formula1 <- y1 ~ Intercept1 + arima1

formula2 <- y2 ~ Intercept2 + arima2

 # Likelihoods

like1 <- like(formula1,

    data = mydata,

    family = "gaussian")

 like2 <- like(formula2,

    data = mydata,

    family = "gaussian")

 # Fitting

fit <- bru(cmp1,

           like1,

           like2)

summary(fit)

I have tried to conduct same for replicate but without success. I’ve tried with a similar structure than before, but now, changing cmp1, formula1 and formula2.

#Effects

r <- rep(1:2, each = n)

cmp1 <- ~ Intercept1 +

  Intercept2  + myar1(map = t, model = "ar1", replicate = r, n = n, values = 1:n)

# Formula

formula1 <- y1 ~ Intercept1 + myar1(map = t, model = "ar1",

                                    replicate = r, n = n, values = 1:n)

formula2 <- y2 ~ Intercept2 + myar1(map = t, model = "ar1",

                                    replicate = r, n = n, values = 1:n)

It would be nice if you could help me in solving the issue.

Thanks,

Joaquín.

messages.body_plain:
In the latest version, the code gave me these messages:

"
Warning in add_mapper(component$main, label = component$label, lhoods = lh,  :
  All covariate evaluations for 'Intercept1' are NULL; an intercept
component was likely intended.
  Implicit latent intercept component specification is deprecated
since version 2.1.14.
  Use explicit notation '+ Intercept1(1)' instead.
Warning in add_mapper(component$main, label = component$label, lhoods = lh,  :
  All covariate evaluations for 'Intercept2' are NULL; an intercept
component was likely intended.
  Implicit latent intercept component specification is deprecated
since version 2.1.14.
  Use explicit notation '+ Intercept2(1)' instead.
Warning in handle_problems(e_input) :
  The input evaluation 'Intercept1' for 'Intercept1' failed. Perhaps
the data object doesn't contain the needed variables? Falling back to
'1'.
Warning in handle_problems(e_input) :
  The input evaluation 'Intercept2' for 'Intercept2' failed. Perhaps
the data object doesn't contain the needed variables? Falling back to
'1'.
"

You're using old, deprecated behavior; as the warnings in this case
accurately say, you need to be specific about the component inputs.
I would suggest the following change:

cmp1 <- ~ 0 + Intercept1(1) +     Intercept2(1) +

    + arima1(t, model = "ar1") +
    + arima2(t, copy = "arima1", fixed = FALSE)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Then second model, are you trying to use one replicate for y1, and
another for y2?
The natural approach is to supply the data that is needed for each
observation model:

mydata1 <- mydata2 <- mydata
mydata1$repl <- 1
mydata2$repl <- 2

cmp1 <- ~ 0 + Intercept1(1) + Intercept2(1) +

  myar(t, model = "ar1", replicate = repl)

# Formula

formula1 <- y1 ~ Intercept1 + myar

formula2 <- y2 ~ Intercept2 + myar

like1 <- like(formula1,
              data = mydata1,

              family = "gaussian")

like2 <- like(formula2,

              data = mydata2,

              family = "gaussian")

fit <- bru(cmp1,
           like1,
           like2)
summary(fit)

> > If you really want the exected value, then you can compute it two ways,
> >
> > for example, let z=exp(x), we have have density for x and want the

I have constructed a mesh using the inla.mesh.2d function.
The inputs are in the same CRS, and the mesh seems to be made and plots nicely, with the following code:
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = CNP,
loc=st_coordinates(final2),
      max.edge = c(1,2)*max.edge,
                  offset=c(max.edge, bound.outer),
                  cutoff = max.edge/5,
                    crs = crs(final2))

However, when I fit the lgcp model, I get this error:
> fit <- lgcp(
components = cmp,
data = nests_,
samplers = transects,
domain = list(
coordinates = mesh,

[1] TRUE

[1] FALSE

What would be the fix for this? I've tried to transform the Mesh CRS but doesn't seem to be working.
Thanks!

messages.subject: Issues running SPDE models more than once with Microsoft Visual C++ error
messages.subject_clean: Issues running SPDE models more than once with Microsoft Visual C++ error
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm working on a project looking at mosquito abundance in Greece. For this I have point locations of mosquito traps and have been running an SPDE model with the formulation below:

form <- y ~ 0 + b0 + f(s, model = spde1)

mod1 <- inla(form,
             family = "poisson",
             data = inla.stack.data(stack.out),
             control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE,
                                      A = inla.stack.A(stack.out)),
             control.compute = list(dic = TRUE))

If I run it a first time after opening a session it usually runs fine. But if I try to rerun it, with or without changing parameters, then it won't run and I get the error box in the image. I then have to close R and restart the session if I want to modify the model (such as changing the family type or adding variables).  This box is then followed by the error message in the console below:
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() : The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully. If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.  *** inla.core.safe: inla.program has crashed: rerun to get better initial values. try=1/2 Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() : The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully. If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.  *** inla.core.safe: inla.program has crashed: rerun to get better initial values. try=2/2 *** inla.core.safe: rerun with improved initial values Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() : The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully. If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

What could cause this? Is this a RAM issue?

Thank you and best regards,
Jerome

messages.subject: Extreme fitted values and issues including fixed priors
messages.subject_clean: Extreme fitted values and issues including fixed priors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am fitting inla models on datasets of different sampling strategies, including a factor of fixed habitat effects and spatial and temporal parameters, with a view to assessing prediction. I have 100 iterations of each strategy, and for some (i.e. iteration 27, below) there were no samples from one of the habitat classes and the resulting values are extreme in those areas.

e.g. summary(res$summary.fitted.values$mean)
     Min.           1st Qu.            Median           Mean                  3rd Qu.                Max.
0.000e+00     4.000e+00     5.000e+00     1.134e+71          6.000e+00         7.562e+72

I tried to set some more restrictive priors to control this, but the priors don't appear to be affecting the model at all (the results are the same regardless of the priors I set).

dat <- strategy1
it <- subset(dat, dat$iter == 27) # iteration 27 - problematic results, no built factor

fixed.priors <- list(mean.intercept = 0, prec.intercept=1/100, mean = list(hab=0), prec = list(hab=1/10))

# inla
coo <- cbind(it$xcoo, it$ycoo)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc=coo, max.edge = c(2, 4), cutoff = 1)
spde.a <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha=2, constr = T)
indexs <- inla.spde.make.index("s", spde.a$n.spde)
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coo)
coop <- cbind(pred$xcoo, pred$ycoo)
Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coop)
stke <- inla.stack(tag="est", data=list(mos = it$mos),A = list(1, A), effects = list(data.frame(hab = it$hab, time=it$mon), s = indexs))
stkp <- inla.stack(tag = "pred", data = list(mos = NA),A = list(1, Ap), effects = list(data.frame( hab = pred$hab, time=pred$time), s = indexs)) # b0 = rep(1, nrow(sim_mos_pred)),
stkfull <- inla.stack(stke, stkp)
res <- inla(mos ~ hab + f(s, model = spde.a)  + f(time, model = "ar1"),
            family = "nbinomial", control.family = list(link = "log"), data = inla.stack.data(stkfull),
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link=1, A = inla.stack.A(stkfull)),
            control.compute = list(config=T, dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
            control.fixed=fixed.priors)

Can anyone advise or suggest why the fixed priors are not making any difference to the model output? Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Extracting values from LGCP
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Extracting values from LGCP
messages.body_plain:
If you just want a point estimate of the maximum density, then max(pred$mean) would give you that, from a predict call with predictor formula
  ~ exp(the expression for the linear predictor)
I think the vignette already includes such a predict call.

If you want the posterior distribution of the maximum, then using generate() with expression
  ~ max(exp(…))
will give you samples from it.  Using the same formula with predict() will give you summary statistics (posterior mean, std.dev <http://std.dev>, and some quantiles).

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If I understand it correctly, INLA adds a noise term to the Ax -term if one uses control.predictor=list(A=Amatrix)

I think INLA estimates (Ax,x) or something similar, which means the field is doubled.

Is it possible to bypass this "extra extension"? I only want Ax and not x, or x but not calculate Ax, as Ax can be found by calculations "after" performing the main estimation.

Also, constraints can be enforced using the usual rules?
I.e if we want to find(Ax)|Bx=0, we can use the kriging formula. It (roughly) becomes (see Rue's "green"-colored book):

x^*=Ax - AQ^(-1)AB (BAQ^(-1)AB^T)^(-1)(BAx)
(As Ax has variance-covariance matrix AQ^(-1)A)
I have not carried out the calculations carefully, so the above expression may not be 100 % correct.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Noise term added when using A-matrix (control.predictor=list(A=Amatrix)
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Noise term added when using A-matrix (control.predictor=list(A=Amatrix)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A few comments (Haavard answered a different aspect of some of this) :

The control.predictor A matrix doesn’t mean “Ax is estimated”, but rather it defines the link between the latent variables and the observed values, and it’s the latent variables that are estimated.
Further, the way this works internally has changed drastically with the new default inla.mode=“compact”.

In the old inla.mode=“classic” (that used to be the default until ca January 2023), inla did do the explicit double extension. The regular model matrix, let’s call it B (not related to your constraint B ), was linked directly to the latent variables as
eta=B x
and the predictor linked to the observations was
eta*=A eta
and the observations were linked to eta*. Both of those steps had a near-singular connection in the joint precision matrix, and the internal model was for the extended space (observation link, eta*, eta, x).

In the new default “compact” mode that is no longer the case, and the internal model representation work directly with the latent variables x, and the observations are linked directly to ABx.

The resulting internal precision matrix may still have a small added epsilon on the diagonal to avoid the other types of singularities (due to the model components themselves; this is what Haavard mentioned), but the stepwise construction singularities due to the deterministic eta*=A eta connection are no longer there.

Now, your question is also about whether one could work directly with Ax instead (or really ABx ! ), but he main problem with that is that one would typically lose sparsity.
When x has Markov structure, A x usually doesn’t. So it’s usually more efficient to do the computations for x, and then only compute the distributional properties of A x afterwards, which I think is what’s happening internally in the new inla.mode.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Following up on my previous email.

You say that for your simulated data points, you have "all the covariate values are held constant except for distance, which linearly increases." This will probably not be suitable because the combination of a constant covariate value for population density, and a constant coefficient of population density will mean that the effect of population density (B*x) is constant.

Your goal should be to estimate the true population density at the extra simulated points, then estimate your model. That done, you will be able to create your desired scatter plot, which is B_population * x_population versus distance.
-W

> On Jul 11, 2023, at 11:51 AM, Wesley Brooks <wbr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Ian,
> I guess the first (possibly dumb) question is have you've specified a model with spatially-varying coefficients? That is not the default behavior.
>
> Your question isn't totally clear. Specifically, it is not clear whether your model's coefficients vary in space or whether the coefficient is constant but the data (e.g., population) varies in space. If you want to know what is the contribution of population across the spatial domain, where population varies but the coefficient is constant then you will calculate that as B x population, where B is the model's estimated coefficient of population and population is the population count in that particular raster cell (or whatever).
>
> -W

Specifically, it is not clear whether your model's coefficients vary in space or whether the coefficient is constant but the data (e.g., population) varies in space. If you want to know what is the contribution of population across the spatial domain, where population varies but the coefficient is constant then you will calculate that as B x population, where B is the model's estimated coefficient of population and population is the population count in that particular raster cell (or whatever).

-W

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to run a model with the following formula:

formula_total <- list(
  transf_stability ~ + sc_pr_mean_slope +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc"),

  mean_total ~  sc_pr_mean_slope +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc") ,

  transf_stability ~ mean_total +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc") ,

  mean_total ~ transf_stability +
    f(spatial.field2, model = "spde.pc")
)

When I try to build the data stack, I get the error message that the names for data and effects cannot be the same. Is there a solution for that problem?

Data stack:
StackEst1_total <- inla.stack(
  data = list(
    transf_stability = fin_dat$transf_stability,
    mean_total = fin_dat$mean_total
  ),
  A = list(
    1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, A_point, 1
  ),
  effects = list(
    transf_stability = fin_dat$transf_stability,
    mean_total = fin_dat$mean_total,
    sc_pr_mean_slope = fin_dat$sc_pr_mean_slope,
    w = s.index,
    Intercept = rep(1, nrow(fin_dat))
  ),
  tag = "Est"
)

Thanks a lot!
Ramona

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It's not clear what the intent of your model is meant to be; if you
want to run them jointly you need (in the plain inla interface) a
single formula.
The short answer is otherwise to change the names of your response
variables, so that it's clear which ones are used as covariates and
when they're used as response variables.

But the details really depend on what the model you want to implement
is; e.g., is the intent that each response variable should be linked
to the same realisation of a common spatial field component, or that
there should be 4 separate model, each with it's own spatial field?

Or did you want the _estimate_ from one model to be used as the
_input_ of the next one? It's not clear from what you wrote. You'd
need to spell out the model definition without referring to the code
(i.e. preferably in text + maths), in order for anyone to know what
the correct code should look like.  It's impossible to to correct the
code without knowing exactly what the intent is.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ramona,

models 1&3 are just two different models for the same observed values,
and not a coherent joint model. Same thing with 2&4.
Models 3 and 4 can _not_ in themselves be used to determine whether Y1
_affects_ Y2 and/or Y2 _affects_ Y1; they will only tell you something
about their association, and running them jointly with each other
and/or models 1&3 doesn't give you any benefits, so just run them
separately if you want them at all.
Causal structure is not something you can infer from this; it only
gives you estimates of the model parameters _given_ a specific model
structure.

So that leaves models 1 and 2, that are linked by involving the same
spatial field, and only differing in the parameters of the observation
model (so allowing them to have different observation noise variance,
but otherwise being identical, unless you allow the coefficient for
the covariate, sc_pr_mean_slope, to be different for the two models,
for example.  Is that what you are looking for?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it sounds like they're using self-referential regression models, where
the observations are on both sides of the model definition; this is
not the normal statistical regression setup, except in auto-regressive
models.
Since the model definition there is in a different R interface, I
think you really need to write down the "pure" mathematical definition
of the model, with no "R formula" shortcuts. E.g., a normal regression
model (with additive Gaussian observation noise)
with R formula shorthand
  y ~ 1 + x
is really defined mathematically as
  y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_x x_i + \epsilon_i
where \epsilon_i are independent N(0, \sigma_e^2) and \beta_1 and
\beta_x are model parameters.

In a self-referential model, you might have something like this:
  x_i = \beta_1 y_j + a_i
  y_j = \beta_2 x_j + b_j
which can be rewritten as
  [-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] [x; y] = [a; b]
and
  [x; y] = [-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] ^{-1} [a; b]
In this case, the rewrite wasn't really necessary, since all the x and
y values were observed, but in other cases such rewrite may be
necessesary;
the initial formulation can in this cas be implemented by simply
renaming the vectors used on the left hand side (as I mentioned in a
previous reply).

If you can write your desired model on this kind of complete
mathematical form, we'll then be able to tell you how to implement it.

Finn

> think you really need to write down the "pure" mathematical definition
> of the model, with no "R formula" shortcuts. E.g., a normal regression
> model (with additive Gaussian observation noise)
> with R formula shorthand
> y ~ 1 + x
> is really defined mathematically as
> y_i = \beta_1 + \beta_x x_i + \epsilon_i
> where \epsilon_i are independent N(0, \sigma_e^2) and \beta_1 and
> \beta_x are model parameters.
>
> In a self-referential model, you might have something like this:
> x_i = \beta_1 y_j + a_i
> y_j = \beta_2 x_j + b_j
> which can be rewritten as
> [-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] [x; y] = [a; b]
> and
> [x; y] = [-\beta_1, 1; 1, -\beta_2] ^{-1} [a; b]
> In this case, the rewrite wasn't really necessary, since all the x and
> y values were observed, but in other cases such rewrite may be
> necessesary;
> the initial formulation can in this cas be implemented by simply
> renaming the vectors used on the left hand side (as I mentioned in a
> previous reply).
>
> If you can write your desired model on this kind of complete
> mathematical form, we'll then be able to tell you how to implement it.
>
> Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello, Aynaz.

Like you say, DIC/WAIC/CPO/CV all somehow relate to whole model predictive performance. If you are more interested in saying something about the contribution of individual covariates on the response variable, then maybe look at the change in predictive performance as variables are removed or added to a model? Maybe you could use citations below to get variable importance weights? Or maybe you just want the relative magnitude of the effects of different covariates, so you could compute standardized regression coefficients?

Here are some citations to check out:
Gelman, A., Hwang, J. and Vehtari, A., 2014. Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models. Statistics and computing, 24(6), pp.997-1016. Here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1307.5928.pdf
Hooten, M.B. and Hobbs, N.T., 2015. A guide to Bayesian model selection for ecologists. Ecological monographs, 85(1), pp.3-28. Here: https://mhooten.github.io/publications/Hooten_Hobbs_EcolMono_2015.pdf
Vehtari, A., Gelman, A., and Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing. 27(5), 1413–1432. Here: doi:10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4. Online <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4>, arXiv preprint arXiv:1507.04544 <https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.04544>.
Yao, Y., Vehtari, A., Simpson, D., and Gelman, A. (2018). Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions. In Bayesian Analysis, doi:10.1214/17-BA1091. Online <https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ba/1516093227>, arXiv preprint arXiv:1704.02030 <https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.02030>.
Gelman, A., 2008. Scaling regression inputs by dividing by two standard deviations. Statistics in medicine, 27(15), pp.2865-2873. Here: http://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/standardizing7.pdf

Best,
Tim

> You say that for your simulated data points, you have "all the covariate values are held constant except for distance, which linearly increases." messages.body_plain:
I am running a model across multiple datasets. In 99% of the datasets, the model runs fine. But on one dataset this error comes up:

GMRFLib_opt_estimate_hessian: ensure spd for Hessian: mode seems fine GMRFLib_opt_estimate_hessian: set tol=[4.326e-06]. number of negative eigenvalues=[2]

Can anyone help interpret this? Offer advice?

The model looks broadly like this:

inla(y ~
              x +
              f(x2, model = "ar1", replicate = group) +
              a bunch of random effects...
              family = "gaussian", etc...)

I have also tried setting the int.strategy = "eb" in the experimental version, and it then runs succesfuly, but my coeficients on x don't look right (relative to expecation and a simulation)

Tom

messages.subject: Low efficiency on HPC compared to local
messages.subject_clean: Low efficiency on HPC compared to local
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For some reason my INLA computations are running much slower on an HPC cluster than on my local machine, despite using many more resources, for a simple mixed effects model.

Both are running the latest stable version of INLA on R 4.2 (the latest available for the HPC cluster).

The issue is not memory bloat when using many threads, since the HPC computation is even slower when using the same number of threads as the local machine. I have experimented with changing inla.mode to classic, and int.strategy to eb, but it does not improve things. Any idea what could be going on?

If it helps, I attached the logfiles from 2 runs of the same model, one from the local machine (8 cores, 16 GB RAM, took 215.175 seconds) and the HPC (24 cores, 6GB RAM per core, took 949.282 seconds).

Will

messages.body_plain:
Hi, you'll need R-4.3 to take advantage of the newer testing versions,
as we only build for R-4.3 now.

Your PARDISO license is expired hence you're running on the TAUCS
library, which do not support parallel factorisations, hence the
potential for speedup is less. Also there are only 3 hyperpar's which
says the same.

(Hopefully the new PARDISO library, and licence, will be integrated
after summer, but we're also looking at other options. )

So in the optimization step, there is little to gain from more than 6
threads.

In the integration phase, you can benefite from 15 threads, but not
more.

I'm also surprised of the large difference in time. HPC systems and
larger servers, do often run slower than my laptop, say, but can run
larger models/data with ease, way beyond where my laptop halts. This is
the main advantage.

I guess you have installed the 'correct' binary on the HPC, like

	library(INLA)
	inla.binary.install()

and chose the CentOS7 one, I guess. I just wonder if that could make a
difference.

Another source, could be that the HPC runs many jobs in parallel hence
you do not get the machine for yourself as you do with your local
machine

I hope this helps

Best
Havard

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to analise model convergence
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ema,

INLAjoint cannot fit spatial survival models (as you know based on our correspondence).

But as with all Bayesian models the basics hold:
Are the posteriors unimodal?
Are the posteriors different from the priors?
Do the predicted survival probabilities make sense?
etc...

These things are not software specific and should always be checked no matter what you use to perform the Bayesian inference.

messages.body_plain:
I have fitted two inla models. The first I used GLMM and the second I used GAMM. The dataset included NA in the outcome variable so the values will be predicted by the models. I already have fitted values (posterior predictive distribution) for each model.

set.seed(123)
library(INLA)
GLMMfitformula<-MP~factor(UD_1)+factor(UD_2)+factor(UV_1)+factor(UV_2)+factor(UTT_2)+factor(UTT_1)+factor(PMB_1)+factor(TMFP_1)+factor(TMHS_1)+factor(TMHS_2)+factor(TMPMB_2)+factor(TMPMB_3)+factor(TMSW_1)+factor(TAFWC_1)+factor(TPAV_2)+factor(TPAD_2)+factor(TPATT_2)+TCF+AO+TCV+NC+TCL+TCW+f(year, model="iid")+f(ID,model="iid")
GLMMpred<-inla(formula=GLMMfitformula,family="gamma", data=INLApredset,control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,mlik=TRUE,cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE,return.marginals.predictor=TRUE), list(link=1,compute=T))

set.seed(1234)
library(INLA)
GAMMfitformula<-MP~factor(UD_1)+factor(UD_2)+factor(UV_1)+factor(UV_2)+factor(UTT_2)+factor(UTT_1)+factor(PMB_1)+factor(TMFP_1)+factor(TMHS_1)+factor(TMHS_2)+factor(TMPMB_2)+factor(TMPMB_3)+factor(TMSW_1)+factor(TAFWC_1)+factor(TPAV_2)+factor(TPAD_2)+factor(TPATT_2)+f(AO)+f(TCV)+f(NC)+f(TCL)+f(TCW)+f(year)+f(ID)
GAMMpred<-inla(formula=GAMMfitformula,family="gamma", data=INLApredset,control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,mlik=TRUE,cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE, return.marginals.predictor=TRUE), control.predictor=list(link=1,compute=T),verbose=TRUE)
summary(GAMMpred)

I wish to plot posterior predictive distributions of model 1, model 2 and actual values in the same graph so as to compare predictive ability of the two models to the unseen dataset. Can you kincly assist me with command.

In attempt to get such a graph, I plotted the graph using below commands, I didn't get what I wanted but I also failed to interpret the graph obtained. Any assistance will be appreciated.

library(INLAutils)
plot_inla_residuals(GLMMpred,imp1dummytest$MP)
plot_inla_residuals(GAMMpred,imp1dummytest$MP)

messages.body_plain:
easiest is to use posterior.sample, like this

## compute predictive data distributions

n <- 20
x <- rnorm(n)
eta <-  1 + 0.2 * x
y <- rpois(n, exp(eta))
y[n] <- NA

r <- inla(y ~ 1 + x,
          data = data.frame(y, x),
          family = "poisson",
          control.compute = list(config = TRUE),
          control.predictor = list(link = 1))

xx <- inla.posterior.sample(1000, r)
y.pred.fun <- function(idx) {
    rpois(length(Predictor[idx]), exp(Predictor[idx]))
}

yy <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(y.pred.fun, xx, idx = which(is.na <http://is.na>(y)))
hist(unlist(yy), prob = TRUE)

by letting 'idx' be a vector you can do many at the same time., then the
output is a matrix, and you can just do the hist of each row (I think)

see the vignette about inla.posterior.sample.eval

messages.subject: Confusing regarding inla.group.cv
messages.subject_clean: Confusing regarding inla.group.cv
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have run into some confusion regarding the inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv> function. In my understanding a cross validation prediction should only depend on the data from other folds, but it seems the predictions in cv$mean are affected by the data in its own fold. This is clear from one of the groups be a large outlier. I hope it is clear what I mean from the plots in the below toy example. Have I misunderstood what the function is supposed to do, or did I maybe misspecify the groups (I followed the vignette)?

n = 50
grp.len = 5
x = rnorm(n)
g = rnorm(grp.len)

g[1] = 200 # Outlier to detect "cheating"

grp = rep(1:grp.len, each = n %/% grp.len)
y = 1 + x + g[grp] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.01)

dat = data.frame(y, x, grp)

df_grp = as.data.frame(matrix(rep(NA, ncol(dat) * grp.len),
                              ncol = ncol(dat)))
colnames(df_grp) <- colnames(dat)
df_grp$grp = 1:grp.len

dat_ext = rbind(dat, df_grp)

r = inla(y ~ x + f(grp, model = "iid"),
         data = dat_ext,
         control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

groups <- lapply(1:(dim(dat_ext)[1]),
                 function(i) which(dat_ext$grp == dat_ext$grp[i]))

cv <- inla.group.cv <http://inla.group.cv>(r, groups = groups)

# Proof of cheating:
#plot(r$summary.fitted.values$mean[1:50]) # "allowed" cheating
#plot(r$summary.fitted.values$mean[51:55]) # "allowed" cheating
#plot(r$summary.random$grp$mean) # "allowed" cheating
plot(cv$mean[1:50]) # Cheating
plot(cv$mean[51:55]) # Cheating

When I used the following code for the construction of the mesh, I found that the dense triangular mesh does not cover my study area (the part within the green boundary). In the middle of the study area, the dense triangular mesh was replaced by a sparse triangular mesh.
my code:
boundary_coords = as.matrix(boundary_coords)
bnd = inla.nonconvex.hull(boundary_coords)
mesh = inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bnd,max.edge=c(0.03,0.1),cutoff=0.01,offset=-0.2)
In this, the green dots are the boundary.
My question is how to change the code to make the centre of my study area also a dense triangular mesh instead of a sparse one?
Thanks for your help!

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to make the MESH boundary extend inwards？
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to make the MESH boundary extend inwards？
messages.body_plain:
The inla.nonconvex.hull algorithm constructs a buffer region around the given point set, so in this case you can solve it by adding a point in the middle (where the hole appeared) to the point set you’re giving to inla.nonconvex.hull, or to add the red dots from you plot to it; since there are several of the in the hole, that should get rid of it.

There’s also a new algorithm that will be available in the new fmesher package that avoids this issue when provided with a polygon as input; it’s already available via the inlabru development package. See
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/reference/fm_nonconvex_hull.html <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/reference/fm_nonconvex_hull.html?q=Noncon#null>

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I have discussed this case with Zhedong (cc'ed above), and it seems that
the impact of '200' is simply to large to be able to compute the cv with
'adjusting' the joint estimate. in particular, the changes '200' have on
the hyperparameters is the main driver, and if you fix the
hyperparmeters and rerun the examples, then you're results will look way
better.

the current computations of the cv or group.cv <http://group.cv>, all assumes that we can
correct the joint estimate to get the estimate when y[i] is removed
(this also includes the hyperparaemters). this implicitely assumes that
the posterior |y and |y[-i]  are not to far away, which is not the case
in your example.

Best
Havard

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatially-varying effects of individual covariates for r-inla
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatially-varying effects of individual covariates for r-inla
messages.body_plain:
This sounds like you just need to do some posterior sampling; the easiest approach to this kind of evaluation I know of is to use the inlabru interface for estimation. That then allows you to do posterior sampling and predictor expression evaluation for given values of the covariates.

Finn

On Fri, 21 Jul 2023, 07:58 'Ian McGregor' via R-inla discussion group, <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Hi Wesley (and others),
>
> First of all, apologies for the lack of clarity in my previous messages. I believe this will make more sense.
>
> In the `margins` package, I am able to fit a standard glm, and then plot the marginal effects of one variable (e.g. population) against specific values of another variable (e.g. distance to town). The plot looks like this.
>
>
>
> To re-create this plot using outputs from INLA, is my only option to do as you suggested, which is simulate some training points at those specific values of distance to town, predict for those points based on the full model, and then extract the marginal effects for population for those?
>
> On Thu, Jul 13, 2023 at 1:29 PM Ian McGregor <imc...@ncsu.edu> wrote:

> >
> > Apologies for the lack of clarity in my question. Your suggestion makes sense, and I will pursue that further.
> >

> > > Following up on my previous email.
> > >
> > > You say that for your simulated data points, you have "all the covariate values are held constant except for distance, which linearly increases." This will probably not be suitable because the combination of a constant covariate value for population density, and a constant coefficient of population density will mean that the effect of population density (B*x) is constant.
> > >
> > > Your goal should be to estimate the true population density at the extra simulated points, then estimate your model. That done, you will be able to create your desired scatter plot, which is B_population * x_population versus distance.
> > > -W

> > > > Hi Ian,
> > > > I guess the first (possibly dumb) question is have you've specified a model with spatially-varying coefficients? That is not the default behavior.
> > > >
> > > > Your question isn't totally clear. Specifically, it is not clear whether your model's coefficients vary in space or whether the coefficient is constant but the data (e.g., population) varies in space. If you want to know what is the contribution of population across the spatial domain, where population varies but the coefficient is constant then you will calculate that as B x population, where B is the model's estimated coefficient of population and population is the population count in that particular raster cell (or whatever).

> > > > > Following up on my previous email.

> > > > > You say that for your simulated data points, you have "all the covariate values are held constant except for distance, which linearly increases." This will probably not be suitable because the combination of a constant covariate value for population density, and a constant coefficient of population density will mean that the effect of population density (B*x) is constant.
> > > > >
> > > > > Your goal should be to estimate the true population density at the extra simulated points, then estimate your model. That done, you will be able to create your desired scatter plot, which is B_population * x_population versus distance.
> > > > > -W

> > > > > > On Jul 11, 2023, at 11:51 AM, Wesley Brooks <wbr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:

> > > > > > Hi Ian,
> > > > > > I guess the first (possibly dumb) question is have you've specified a model with spatially-varying coefficients? That is not the default behavior.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Your question isn't totally clear. Specifically, it is not clear whether your model's coefficients vary in space or whether the coefficient is constant but the data (e.g., population) varies in space. If you want to know what is the contribution of population across the spatial domain, where population varies but the coefficient is constant then you will calculate that as B x population, where B is the model's estimated coefficient of population and population is the population count in that particular raster cell (or whatever).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > -W

messages.body_plain:
I'm tyring to get  a spacetime model from
chapter 11 of Ravishankar et al,
"Dynamic Time Series Models using R-INLA" to run
under inla.knmodels, but I get an error message
I can't understand.

Here's the setup:
library(INLA)

# load the data and space graph
load("c:/work/R/ravishanker/Chapter11/data_kh.Rdata") # loads data.kh <http://data.kh>
nyc.adj <- inla.read.graph(filename = "c:/work/R/ravishanker/Chapter11/map.adj")

# set up the spacetime index
data.kh <http://data.kh>$id.spacetime<-1:nrow(data.kh <http://data.kh>)

# base formula, without spacetime effect
formula.base <-
  tnc.month ~ 1 + f(id.zone, model = "bym", graph = nyc.adj) +
  f(id.month, model = "rw1") +
  f(id.monthu, model = "iid")

# now a non-spacetime model:
tnc.kh0<-inla(formula.base,data=data.kh <http://data.kh>,
      control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
      control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
      family = "poisson")
summary(tnc.kh0)
# this closely matches the result in the book.

# now let's try a type-1 knmodel
tnc.kh1 <- inla.knmodels(
  formula.base,data = data.kh <http://data.kh>,  control.st <http://control.st>=list(time=id.month,space=id.zone,spacetime=id.spacetime,graph=nyc.adj,type=1),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
  family = "poisson"
)
Error in inla.knmodels(formula.base, data = data.kh <http://data.kh>, control.st <http://control.st> = list(time = id.month,  :
  object 'n' not found

#####################

So my question is: what is the "n" that inla.knmodels is looking for
but not finding?

Thanks for any guidance.

I've taken a look at the code for inla.knmodels
and run my failing problem under debug. Here's
the block of code that seems to generate the problem:

    if (!is.null(space)) {
        if (!is.null(mcall$control.st <http://control.st>$graph)) {
            if (n != length(unique(space))) {
                stop("Size of 'space' is not equal to the size of 'graph'!")
            }
        }
        n <- length(unique(space))
    }

When I get here, (!is.null(space)) is TRUE
                 (!is.null(mcall$control.st <http://control.st>$graph)) is TRUE
So we want to compare n to length(unique(space))
length(unique(space)) is 252
But n seems not to be defined, and I can't see anywhere
in the preceding code where it is set.

Could the problem arise from the use of package sf to
create the adjacency matrix, which is the way the
shape file is processed for my problem? Namely,
the sequence here is:

zoneshape<-st_read([shape file])  # st_read from package sf
nb.q<-poly2nb(zoneshape,queen=TRUE,row.names=zoneshape$zone.id <http://zone.id>)
nb2INLA("map.adj",nb.q)
nyc.adj<-inla.read.graph(filename="map.adj")

nyc.adj has an element nyc.adj$n which is (correctly) 252
but as I say, at that point in inla.knmodels n seems undefined.

I should add here that the example in the help for inla.knmodels
runs with no problems.

messages.body_plain:
I think I may have solved the problem. In the
code for inla.knmodels we have:

    if (!is.null(space)) {
        if (!is.null(mcall$control.st <http://control.st>$graph)) {
            if (n != length(unique(space))) {
                stop("Size of 'space' is not equal to the size of 'graph'!")
            }
        }
        n <- length(unique(space))
    }

When we come to evaluate
  if (n != length(unique(space)))
n is not provided via computations in inla.knmodels.
It is therefore sought in the user's global
environment. At least, setting n globally avoids
the 'n' not found message.

Is this correct?  If so, then the puzzling thing about
this fragment is the expression   n <- length(unique(space)).
If we get through
  if (!is.null(mcall$control.st <http://control.st>$graph)
without hitting the stop, then we know that n has this value,
so why do we set it explicitly again?

Be that as it may, my problem now generates a different
error, namely

Error in h(simpleError(msg, call)) :
  error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for function
  'which': 'list' object cannot be coerced to type 'integer

This seems to be generated by the line

j.s <- which(r.size == .no.of.s)

in my case .no.of.s is 252 ( = n) while r.size is
a 2-element list, both of whose elements are NULL.
Presumably this has to do with something going wrong
with the structure or data of the problem I'm working
with - does it suggest what that might be? What
should r.size be measuring?

Thanks for any ideas!

messages.subject: How to automatic select the optimal covariates？
messages.subject_clean: How to automatic select the optimal covariates？
messages.body_plain:
In INLA, is there a way to automatically select the best combination of environment variables？Manual selection of covariates is very tedious.
For example, I have the following formula:
y ~ x1+x2+x3+x4......+x10+……
But obviously, this combination of variables is not optimal. Currently, the method I use to filter the variable combinations is to remove the covariates one by one and compare their DIC values and select the combination with the lowest DIC. But obviously, this method is cumbersome if there are too many variables. So is there any way to automate the selection of the optimal combination of variables in INLA?

Am I expected to put each year in a separate column and consider it as an independent variable while constructing the formula?
I would be happy if you send me example codes for spatiotemporal analysis in INLA.
Thank you!
Wubet

messages.body_plain:
I'm glad to report that the testing version of
inla.knmodels  (23.06.29) solved the n-not-found
problem from a previous posting. But I'm still having
trouble getting any knmodel setup to work.

Here's an example, drawn from Ch 7 of Blangiardo+Cameletti

################### R code begins

library(INLA)
inla.setOption(scale.model.default=FALSE)

set.seed(12345)
require(maptools)

my.dir <- "c:/work/R/blangiardo/"

################### setup for work: this code is from the book
################### or the code from the book website

data <- read.csv(paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/data.final.csv",sep=""))
georgia <- readShapePoly(paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/co13_d00.shp",sep=""))

# Remove duplicates (area 88 and 94)
names <- georgia$NAME
georgia <- georgia[-c(99,100,105,137),]
data.georgia <- attr(georgia, "data")

low.vector <- as.vector(as.matrix(data[,2:12])) #by column
E.vector <- as.vector(as.matrix(data[,13:23]))  #by column
year <- numeric(0)
for(i in 1:11){
  year<- append(year,rep(i,dim(data)[1]))
}

# county replicates the county names 11 times
county <- as.factor(rep(data[,1],11))

data <- data.frame(y= low.vector, E= E.vector, ID.area=as.numeric(county),
                   ID.area1=as.numeric(county), year=year,
                   ID.year = year, ID.year1=year, ID.area.year = seq(1,length(county)))

# Spatial graph
Georgia.adj <- paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/Georgia.graph",sep="")
# Temporal graph
Temp.adj <- paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/Temp.graph",sep="")

data$ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int> <- data$ID.area
data$ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int> <- data$ID.year

######################### now a Type-I model as in the book

formula.intI<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym", graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") + f(ID.year1,model="iid") + f(ID.area.year,model="iid")

mod.intI <- inla(formula.intI,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

print(summary(mod.intI))
# runs fine

####################### next, try to set up for knmodels

data$ID.spacetime<-1:nrow(data)

# formula.base is formula.int1 minus the spacetime spec (last term)
formula.base<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym", graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") + f(ID.year1,model="iid")

mod.kh1<-inla.knmodels(formula.base,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
               control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
               control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),
               control.st <http://control.st>=list(time=ID.year1, space=ID.area,
                     spacetime=ID.spacetime, graph=Georgia.adj, type=c(1)),
               control.inla=list(strategy='gaussian')  )
Error in h(simpleError(msg, call)) :
  error in evaluating the argument 'x' in selecting a method for
  function 'which': 'list' object cannot be coerced to type 'integer'

################### R code ends.  comments/ questions

1. Is my translation of the book model to the knmodel correct?
2. I get this error message doing the same thing for
   a model in the Ravishankar "Dynamic Time Series Models ... " book.
3. Omitting the control.inla spec doesn't help.

messages.subject: Non-stationary-binomial response
messages.subject_clean: Non-stationary-binomial response
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm trying to implement a spatial non-stationary model using a binomial response. I'm adapting a piece of code from Ingebrigtsen, Lindgren, and Steinsland (2014), where the response is precipitation (gaussian), to Gambia's malaria cases dataset from the geoR package, which is explained in Moraga (2020). I'm aware that the selection of hyperparameters values is crucial in this kind of model, and the ones I'm using (corresponding to the original paper) are not proper for the selected data, but I'm also sure that there are other silly mistakes. I will appreciate it if you can point these out for me in order to achieve the estimation. I will also appreciate any recommendations for the selection of hyperparameter values, considering that the original priors are very informative. The following code corresponds to the model fitting step, but I'm attaching the complete code with the necessary data in order to reproduce the example. Thank you in advance for your help an guidance.

# Non-stationary:
formula.ns = y ~ -1 +
  f(intercept,
    model = "linear",
    mean.linear = 0,
    prec.linear = 0.0001) +
  f(elevation,
  model = "linear",
  mean.linear = 0,
  prec.linear = 0.0001) +
  f(field, model = spde.ns)

result.ns = inla(formula.ns,
                 family = "binomial",
                 Ntrials = numtrials,
                 data = inla.stack.data(data.stack),
                 control.predictor = list(
A = inla.stack.A(data.stack),
compute = TRUE,
link = 1),
                 control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE,
                                        dic = TRUE),
                 control.family = list(link = "logit"),
                 #control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma", param = c(2,0.02)))),
                 control.inla = list(h = 1e-4,
                                     tolerance = 1e-8),
                 verbose = TRUE
)

I would try with

r=inla(..., control.inla=list(cmin=0))

r$.args$control.inla$cmin <- -Inf
r = inla.rerun(r)

usually this make solve the issue.

the zero-inflated ones are not log-concave in all parameters, hence the
issue...

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
you can also use the slm model in a joint model, but you have to be
careful as the 'slm' model is using a fake likelihood to achive it.
please refer to one of the (free-)books on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> for how to setup
joint models (or models with more than one likelihood)

Best
H
